Interviewer:	OK I’ll tell you a bit about what we’re doing. The project involves interviewing quite a few different women engineering students, and we’re asking them about why they decided to do engineering and their education so far and about why they wanted to do the placement and things like that. And then we’ll go again to interview students while they’re on placement, to find out how it’s going. And we’re basically trying to sort of improve women’s retention in the engineering industry. Things like that – and whether what actually happens in industry is what you expect. Then eventually we’re going to produce a document of guidelines that we’re going to give back to the engineering industry, hopefully to improve things for women. OK, I’ll start off then just asking some background questions about why you decided to do engineering and things like that. Are you doing chemical engineering?

Subject:	Yeah, I’m doing chemical engineering.

Interviewer:	OK. Did you do ‘A’ levels?

Subject:	A levels, no. I didn’t do ‘A’ levels – I did (?) for 3 years. It’s similar to doing ‘A’ levels.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do those in different subjects?

Subject:	Er, well I took pure science and pure maths (OK) but it pretty much covers exactly the same thing as ‘A’ levels – (lost words)

Interviewer:	OK, what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Er before university (Yeah) Well I did normal, secondary school so GCE – O levels and then after that I went to private college to do Canadian (Pre-U?) and (lost words)

Interviewer:	OK, was that a mixed school or an all girls school?

Subject:	Er, a mixed college. A mixed co-ed school.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got any previous work experience in the engineering industry?

Subject:	No, no I haven’t.

Interviewer:	OK, what do your parents do? Are either of them engineers?

Subject:	Oh my mum has a (?) for women engineer.

Interviewer:	OK, how long have you been in Britain for?

Subject:	Oh, I just came last September

Interviewer:	Right, OK.

Subject:	This year.

Interviewer:	So did you start university at another?

Subject:	I did, while I was at college, I went to this type of training programme, that you could sort of compress like of one year to, into eight months. At the moment, (lost words) so I did the first year in 8 months and (?) in September, so I start the second year (?) after my first year.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s great. When and why then do you think that you decided to study engineering?

Subject:	Oh, I thought it would be interesting and it has more – it’s more mathematically – mathematically based, yeah, compared to the other degrees. And I’m not really interested in sort of business and social science, that kind of – it’s like, er, there are more job opportunities like now in the engineering sector industry and it’s challenging so I think I like.

Interviewer:	OK. What bits of engineering do you think that you find interesting?

Subject:	What bits of my course?

Interviewer:	Yeah. Before you started your course, why did you think that it would be interesting?

Subject:	Oh, the maths was interesting – yeah. Well, other than that, the things that we study like maybe some (?), like we work in a tradition – like we are hard but it’s nice to look at things and think mm, we can do that, we can do that and so it’s fine. In a way – I mean it hasn’t read that much – it’s only like a couple of years out – that takes (?) the courses that you have. You have to read and re(?) and not so much for engineering.

Interviewer:	OK, when did you decide to do engineering? Was it after you’d done the ‘A’ level equivalent or was it before?

Subject:	It was half way – the middle – doing the ‘A’ level equivalent, ‘cos I was thinking of – actually I thought bio technology, prior to engineering, then I – some problem came up so I thought it wasn’t right me doing bio technology because it’s dealing with going against nature, so then I thought oh engineering, but quite, but it was after doing all along some (?) like – erm, the last week of the engineer and the transition would not be so bad.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there were any other influences like the fact that your father’s in engineering?

Subject:	Uh huh. I think my father was the one that introduced this engineering thing. He didn’t really tell me about what he’s doing – but I know he’s an engineer, so it tells me that this profession and also like friends – my friends – my siblings and friends, yeah friends, people in the – you know – kind of engineering as well, so that’s how I got into this thing.

Interviewer:	Yeah, Ok.

Subject:	Oh yeah, and also because there are more girls in chemical engineering than the other engineering departments. Yeah.

Interviewer:	So is that something that you considered?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely.

Interviewer:	OK, I’ll probably come back to that in a bit. When you were applying for the courses, did you know that you wanted to do a sandwich course?

Subject:	Yes, I was – that was why I came to [this university] actually being a – because I want to go for a placement.

Interviewer:	OK, were there any other reasons that you decided to come to [this university]?

Subject:	Any other reasons? Well the – the fact that they had really good relationship with the industry. And also that engineering is part of the same – quite – well the chemical engineering department is really quite tiny, than all the others. Erm, [university town] is a nice place, quiet, not a big city.

Interviewer:	OK, you said that you probably chose chemical engineering because there were more women on that course (yeah). Did it bother you that engineering was so male dominated?

Subject:	Mm, it only bothered me in the sense that part of me – I would have been the only girl in class. Er, not so much the fact that there are so many males in industry, yeah. It is a fact that there are more male engineers than women engineers and hardly know any women engineers.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged to study engineering?

Subject:	Mm, er I don’t know what to say, I think most of them think that it’s – I suppose that you have to wear – your groups helmet in (lost words) So that’s all women who have the potential. I think that it will be good to do just as well as men on the (?) – yeah. I think it would be good for the industry too.

Interviewer:	Do you think that anything could be done in engineering – say in education, to encourage more women to take engineering?

Subject:	Oh yeah, like I think the women engineering society (?) mentoring thing to girls who are like – I’m not really sure if its 10 to 14 to talk to the girls – tell them more about what we’re doing. I think that’s a really nice approach to introduce girls to engineering, ‘cos I think at that age – probably I thought about what I wanted to do, at that age. So yeah, I’d just like to tell them that it’s not about the whole of that (lost words)

Interviewer:	Do you think that with your father being in engineering, that sort of opened up the profession up to you? Do you think that people just don’t know what engineering is to even contemplate it in the first place?

Subject:	Yeah, I would say that they don’t really know what engineering is. I didn’t know 100% what engineering’s all about until I did it myself and I spoke to those people who are already graduated. Yeah, I think that you can – we have a laugh, it’s only an engineer, you didn’t have to go out – (lost words)

Interviewer:	OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Hmm, oh you must (pause) you have to be flexible and we have to think of our decisions – good decisions and think clear. And also, you are academic I think because people they think it’s not tough, associated with engineers, it’s tough – it’s hard work doing engineering subjects because there’s so much involved and decision making and so if you are not – if you’re not at – how you say? – sparking and like a small (?) – I don’t think you can make those decisions.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those characteristics you would say are more male or more female characteristics?

Subject:	I think they are more male characteristics – yeah, ‘cos they are more daring – males. They tend to throw out like really – like be arrogant. They are always – they’re adventurous – they tend to be – try more things. Girls tend to stick to the more conventional really – more safe proven ways.

Interviewer:	That’s interesting. Do you think that there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Disadvantage. Well the only disadvantage that I can think of is less of female group. But the advantage is I think you manage to get to see – like you get to – how do I say? – you get to experience what the other sex is, what they do. Like if they look across you a bit, it’s like you should show your authority – let them know you’re on a par on with them.

Interviewer:	Do you think because you’re a woman you sometimes have to work harder to prove yourself?

Subject:	Not really. 

Interviewer:	Has the course been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	More than what I expected. 

Interviewer:	And what do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	The best thing about the course right now I think would be the opportunity that you have in engineering to do the design coursework well I think 4 times more than what my friends have where they are at [name] University – they have 1 and that’s all. The (?) last one, it lasts the whole year and I remember not doing this time when I didn’t do coursework last – and when we’re getting to do some companies, and we look at businesses, if you can give them really good feedback, like all of us (?) yeah, this year we have the coursework.

Interviewer:	Yeah. And is there anything bad about the course?

Subject:	There is much work but I take it that’s good. It is really bad but you learn a lot from the course. We didn’t know – there was this module, last semester, that we aren’t really used to but we did a design project prior to that so it’s different and really varied (lost words) and how you are going to apply it and can’t really from that know, and yes, that’s what you do. I really think that I can do things my friends can’t do.

Interviewer:	OK, are you pleased that you decided to do this course then?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s good. Have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

Subject:	No. All my lecturers are male.

Interviewer:	Do you find that discouraging at all? Or would you find it encouraging to have been taught by some female lecturers?

Subject:	It would be nice to have women lecturers – woman lecturer, but in a sense you don’t need it, it would be something that, you know…

Interviewer:	Yeah. Have you ever really thought about – you haven’t sort of …?

Subject:	Yeah, I think (?) women, yeah, this is man. I don’t think there’s even a woman lecturer in my department. No.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the lecturers treat the female students differently to the male students?

Subject:	Oh, we have one that treats us – he’s really nice. Ah, other than that I think its pretty much even.

Interviewer:	How many women are there on your course?

Subject:	My course? Erm, 40 female, 60 males.

Interviewer:	That’s quite good. Ok, have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Are they male as well?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Would you rather have had a female personal tutor or doesn’t it bother you either way?

Subject:	No, I like to have a woman personal tutor, but my personal tutor is fine.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that a female personal tutor would be better?

Subject:	Well, I think she’ll probably be more approachable (yeah) yeah. I think sometimes you sit there and he doesn’t know what to ask. Maybe they would be more – make you feel more comfortable.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anything or anybody that you would say has been the greatest influence on you since you started the course?

Subject:	Do you mean academically or?

Interviewer:	Yeah. It doesn’t matter if there hasn’t been.

Subject:	Er, no.

Interviewer:	That’s OK. Has the teaching that you’ve had, involved much group work?

Subject:	Yes, a lot.

Interviewer:	Do you like doing group work?

Subject:	Er, well doing the work isn’t my (?) because I’ve just been – because you work with so many different people and you like you encounter a lot of problems, but I think I like it very much that I learn a lot from it, but that’s purely the fact that – well, yeah.

Interviewer:	What do you think are the benefits of doing group work?

Subject:	Oh er, first things you get to share the load. Second that it doesn’t always (?) – secondly you – well you do develop some leadership skills and your team working skills and also your communication skills.

Interviewer:	Do you think they’re useful when you’re applying for jobs?

Subject:	Yes, very very.

Interviewer:	OK, when you’re working in groups, how do you decide who to work with?

Subject:	How? We don’t decide – it gets decided for us. So, at each time we’ve got a bit more – like 5 different people, so you know, it’s always – the fact is it’s 5 different people – quite hard sometimes but it’s alright, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you prefer to work with men or women or doesn’t it bother you?

Subject:	I prefer to work with communicative people. It doesn’t matter if it’s man or woman.

Interviewer:	OK, have you had any particularly bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Er, except some people not doing their work, not really.

Interviewer:	OK, when the people are not pulling their weight, how do you overcome that?

Subject:	For me, personally, I work – well I used to just take it from them and just do it myself, ‘cos sometimes it gets so frustrating like they just say that they can’t do it, they can’t do it, it’s like they didn’t really try. So like some of the figure – I’m able to do it better than them, so I’ll just take it and do it myself.

Interviewer:	Yes, OK. What aspect of the teaching or advice that you’ve had, do you think will help you when you go on your placement?

Subject:	Ah, not to take the work – not to how you say? – not to do more than your fair share, but solve the problems within your group meetings and not take your problems on your own time. (Lost words) when you go out to work you can’t really – because to get them in you have to pick (lost words) it’s not really fair.

Interviewer:	So don’t take too much on?

Subject:	Don’t take more – don’t bite off more than you can chew (yeah) or so. I think you can solve the problem within the group and not take it as your own problem.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there are lots of skills from the course that you’ll take to the placement with you?

Subject:	A lot of what?

Interviewer:	Skills.

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	And knowledge?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Do you think you will actually use what you’ve learnt on the course?

Subject:	I think I will use because this season I have been (?) exactly what is going to happen and what. (lost words)

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel prepared and ready to go on placement?

Subject:	Quite.

Interviewer:	Are you looking forward to it?

Subject:	Uh huh.

Interviewer:	Have the university done anything to help prepare you for going on your placement?

Subject:	For in working?

Interviewer:	Mm

Subject:	Well, one thing that I could think of is (?) studies and just in – and also we get, for one thing they get the real people to be there to judge how we perform, things like that.

Interviewer:	Have you spoken to any students that have been on placement before?

Subject:	Yeah, I have.

Interviewer:	Did you find that helpful?

Subject:	Er, yeah, we did give some feedback and they did tell you what to expect and what not to expect.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think the way you are taught reflects what life will be like when you are working in the industry?

Subject:	No, maybe not. You never know until you are in there. And it also depends on your working environment.

Interviewer:	OK, so why did you think that the placement was a good idea?

Subject:	Firstly, you expect to get the experience and secondly was – well the thought of working like in a proper big British company is really like – how you say? – you look forward to that, sort of know it is a type of job, you produce some big things.

Interviewer:	Ok, did anyone encourage you or discourage you from going on placement at all?

Subject:	No – my tutor encouraged me to go for placement. And my parents are all for it. No one really discourage me, everyone’s been telling me it’s a really good position.

Interviewer:	OK, Do you know where you’re going on your placement?

Subject:	Yeah, I’ll be in [place], working with [company].

Interviewer:	[Company]?

Subject:	Yeah, doing like – doing aggro-chemicals. They were part of [company] before (lost words).

Interviewer:	What attracted you to that company? How did you decide that one?

Subject:	Well, it’s just that they have more technical – they need more technical support and so I just applied to them – go ahead.

Interviewer:	Did you apply to that – this company?

Subject:	Yeah, I applied to others as well. Actually I was really interested in the petro-chemical but everyone else was interested in those so – yeah, didn’t get that, so, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, when you applied to companies, was it the type of work that they told you that you would be doing that you were interested in, or did you look at things like pay or training opportunities, or the proportions of men and women in the company, or career prospects or anything?

Subject:	I looked at er, to see what they was doing like oil, (?) chemicals, and then I looked at those – the work that we would do. Some of them had like computers and (lost words) and yeah, pay.

Interviewer:	OK, what sort of research into the company did you do? That information that you…

Subject:	Had the Open Day, not the open day, the careers day and also looked up on the web sites and actual like what people said to me.

Interviewer:	OK, how involved were the university in helping find a placement for you?

Subject:	On a scale of 1 to 10, I think about 8.

Interviewer:	They were quite helpful?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	What sort of things did they do?

Subject:	Erm, well the careers helped and things. The department as well – the – actually when we applied to the companies, yeah, its through the department – but all the companies that we know off, they put it up on the board and they say (lost words). Yeah.

Interviewer:	Did you find that was helpful?

Subject:	That was really helpful compared to what I was finding – I had to do, like (?) in industry. They had tick off what they’d done, if they’d approached those companies.

Interviewer:	OK, did you ever consider getting sponsorship at all?

Subject:	By?

Interviewer:	By a company?

Subject:	I like to get one but no I don’t really expect to get one, not from [company] obviously but maybe if its like a bigger company.

Interviewer:	What do you think are the advantages and disadvantages of doing sponsorship?

Subject:	Well, one thing is that you know that you’ve got the company’s attention, that you’d be the – you have the capability to work, yeah but the disadvantage would be you’re stuck with them. Getting money from them is OK for them.

Interviewer:	OK, what sort of thing are you expecting to get out of the placement? What do you think you’ll learn from it?

Subject:	I’ll probably learn how to deal with things but in more mature way. And also er, it probably helps me more in decision making ‘cos I know what I’ll be doing – like in terms of – roughly I’m just guessing, I’m not sure.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think will be the best and the worst things about being on placement? What are you most looking forward to and what are you worried about?
Subject:	Most looking forward to being – doing work, because I haven’t done any real work, and look forward to meeting other people, so you know. Not really worried about anything probably just moving there by myself because I think I will be the only one from the department going.

Interviewer:	Will there be any other students there?

Subject:	Yeah, there are 2 other guys from (lost words).

Interviewer:	Do you think that will help…?

Subject:	Yeah, other placements definitely will help in the sense like less burden and works for me.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you think that being at work will differ from being at university?

Subject:	Ok – if you work you get pay, and also like you get first hand experience and you get to deal with real kind of thing, like now what do we do to is a piece of paper – you don’t really see much.

Interviewer:	Put the things that you’ve learnt into practice. Do you think that the way you are treated will be different?

Subject:	After I come back off placement?

Interviewer:	Or how you’re treated at university, compared to at the placement?

Subject:	Oh maybe at placement you – people will like treat you in more of an adult manner (yeah) whereas university treat you as a kid. (lost words)

Interviewer:	Do you think that what you learn on the placement will help you when you come back for your final year?

Subject:	Yes, I think so – like I don’t know what I’ll be doing but like in (SLP?) but (lost words) have a problem, yeah? If you’re (lost words) but apart from that no thoughts about what could be happening in my final year.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career then, what do you think that you’ll be doing in 5 years time?

Subject:	5 years – I think I’ll still be working as a process engineer, yeah.

Interviewer:	What about in 10 years?

Subject:	10 years? Probably working part time. Erm, I’m not sure but I used to think like my younger brothers study chemical engineer and I was thinking maybe we set up a company and doing consultation work or something like that.

Interviewer:	Why do you think you’ll be doing part time work?

Subject:	Oh, in 10 years, I’ll be 30, ‘cos many women are married and there’s kids and all (laughs) yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there is much opportunity for part time work, in the engineering industry?

Subject:	No, not part-time work – part-time like when I say we have our own company, we have our own – yeah – then you, you’ll be able to take more time off work.

Interviewer:	Does it concern you at all, in the future having to combine sort of family and career?

Subject:	Oh well, if you’re – as far as the training is then I’ll probably say I’m retired, yeah. I’m not really concerning too much (lost words).

Interviewer:	OK, what would be your ideal career?

Subject:	Er, my ideal career would be working for a petro-chemical company and going like – doing all the dirty jobs. Not really dirty but you have to go on site and see things and do the (?). Challenging career is the ideal.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there’ll be any difficulties trying to achieve that ideal career?

Subject:	Er, well if the company is so male dominated and they probably – er see women as a back-up and if they can, use as much male power as…

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that career prospects are good in chemical engineering?

Subject:	Yes, they are – very.

Interviewer:	Yes, OK, that’s good. Are you happy with all the career decisions that you’ve made so far – if you went through it all again would you do anything differently?

Subject:	Erm, (lost words)

Interviewer:	Ok, Do you think when you’ve finished your course, you’ll stay in the UK?

Subject:	Yeah, I’m still thinking of doing research in chemical engineering. I’m not sure what that will be.

Interviewer:	OK, how would you describe the characteristics of the engineering industry in 5 words?

Subject:	Challenging, erm tough, erm, male dominated, very wide industry – very broad – and…interesting really.

Interviewer:	OK, why do you think that it is so male dominated?

Subject:	Mm, probably because in the past, like women – like probably a decade ago, two decades ago when women started to become almost equal and it’s that going into things that normally men do. So, but this – engineering’s mostly men, so…

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that going into a male dominated culture will cause you any problems at all?

Subject:	Well you probably won’t feel so comfortable – maybe if there’s like a 10:1 ratio. Yeah. It also surprised in that when I called up for accommodation in [company] they have a lodge and they told me that the lodge, if I was to stay there it would be fairly awkward for me, because there are 8 males in there and 2 girls. So yeah, it’s probably that kind of problem I think.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that as an engineering student your educational experience is the same as for social sciences or business?

Subject:	Er, I think yeah. It’s just that er it’s like for social sciences you have more – I don’t know – pieces of – pieces of (?) that need (?) – the industry will be less – very lighter – how do you say? Not so intensive kind of work that you find in engineering students. And it’s not one that, like people – in which all the people see what they can do. You can but maybe you won’t be able to put it into (?) – the best use of study is if you’ve had it.

Interviewer:	 (lost words)

Subject:	Yeah, but more reading you’re having, but if you’re doing engineering stuff, you have to do it very (?) – yeah, more technical things to do.

Interviewer:	So do you think that the course you’re doing will prepare you better for when you go to work, than say a social science degree?

Subject:	Social science – I’m not sure about social science but I believe they only take more (?) on social science but maybe if you’re doing business studies and stuff (lost words).

Interviewer:	OK, that’s everything thank you very much.
